Anti-War and Anti Military. Two positions that should be adopted at once( since it is only logical to hate the men, the military who carry out the acts of war) but isn’t always. Hollywood has fed us with anti-war, pro-military narratives for decades and this continues in that tradition. “Good Soldier, bad commander” is the  easy and non offensive pill for the average American movie goer to swallow while still maintaining the veneer of a daring picture. When Clint shows us troops barging into a horrified families house, I think it’s easy to infer that he doesn’t see this as something to be proud of. It’s disgusting, ugly, and uncomfortable. Clint has been pretty consistently anti-war and it’s clear he views the war on terror as a useless farce that helped barely anyone. He checks off the anti-war box  , but anti- military? far from it. You’d think this would be a Taxi Driver type affair where you see a sick and twisted man devolve further and further into his appetite for blood, and the film does fulfill to a certain degree. Chris Kyle becomes a walking corpse in the middle, only feeling fulfilled when he’s at war and feeling empty elsewhere. It’s a tragedy for sure, but who’s tragedy? The millions of citizens murdered during the war or the sniper who committed it all? It’s  called “American Sniper” for a reason. Clint’s central conceit is that the Chris Kyle tragedy is of him being pulled away  from his family and having to see his friends die. Iraqi’s are barely human, being reduced to flocks of people whose children have instincts to pick up rocket launchers, definitely realistic and not hitlerite eugenics garbage. They only become victims at the hands of “the butcher”, an OC Eastwood and co inserted into what’s supposed to be a harrowing account of real event. What is presented to us is this: Kyle is a broken but good man who was simply thrown into a war he had little in-depth  knowledge of, which eventually became too much for him. He hates the war and after the events of his fourth tour, he wishes only to go back to his family. Everything in the above sentences is bullshit. In the real world, Kyle bragged about the murders he committed and even made up fake and unproven scenarios of murdering random people. It’s so egregious, he lied about killing people who were trying to survive during Katrina. The mistake Eastwood makes is thinking Kyle ever stopped loving war and battle(he never did) or ever felt guilt( he felt pride about his service). Clint is too attached to the military to make this anything worth while, he's too obsessed to separate the individual from the system that validates his terror. The individual is presented as the victim and not the willing pawn he really was. The fact that this movie has been so thoroughly embraced by politicians I thinks speaks enough. They aren’t misunderstanding the text, a text that venerates troops as broken men simply doing what they think to be right, men who were “just following orders”, wait, where have I heard that before……. “Good soldier Bad Commander” is functionally still propaganda just with a kinder coat of paint that wants to trick you into believing it’s important.

Even ignoring the contents of the book, do some research into the stuff Chris Kyle has talked about outside the war. For example, he claimed that during Hurricane Katrina, he and another fellow sniper travelled to New Orleans, posted up atop the Superdome, and proceeded to shoot “dozens” of “armed” residents. This is not just a person affected by the fervor of 9/11 and blinded by hate. This is a sociopath. People like Chris Kyle have no business being honored and lauded by our government, our media or our people. The movie even tries to hide the truth, portraying Kyle as a traumatized war veteran who is haunted by his time in Iraq. The truth is, according to Kyle himself, he loved the war, and he loved killing. This is a disgusting movie based on a disgusting book and should never be taken seriously by anyone except psychologists looking to peer into the mind of a sick, bloodthirsty killer. This is going to be a long one and I'll have to write it over multiple sessions, so I apologise if it ends up coming across as scattered. I have a fervent hatred toward Chris Kyle, his book, and this movie. American Sniper is torturous to watch (and read) because it simply enrages me, but I forced myself to do so again for this review. My first viewing was a few years ago alongside my reading of his book of the same name. To preface this review, I feel it necessary to state my moral positioning with regards to the Iraq War. I don't agree with the take that all soldiers are inherently evil or some such. I've met some great people in the armed forces, and like many things in life, it cannot be looked at from a simplistic black and white lens. I have a lot of admiration for the bravery of many men and women that risk and sacrifice their lives to protect their country and save lives. There are many incredible people in those roles, and there are unfortunately also a number of disgusting pieces of shit like Chris Kyle. Likewise, there were many terrorists on the Iraqi side, but also lots of freedom fighters resisting the US led invasion of their country. The problem with American Sniper (aside from Chris himself) is that it has no such nuance, and even goes so far as to deliberately simplify the conflict. American Sniper would be a middling film even if consumed in a vacuum, but that isn't possible with a movie based on a "true story", no matter how much actor and producer Bradley Cooper absurdly claims it is "not a political movie at all". Director Clint Eastwood similarly argues that this is an anti-war film, which is absolutely ridiculous. Take the opening scene for example. In the movie, Chris spots a woman hand an explosive to her son and sends him to his death in an attempt to blow up the American troops. While the book and Chris's accounts on the likes of talk shows differ, at no point did he claim that the woman he killed handed her child said explosive. This was a deliberate retelling of events by Eastwood that can only be interpreted as trying to make the Iraqis clear evil, in order to make viewers sympathise with the American soldiers. Right from the outset of the film, they make a clear distinction on which side is right and the other in the wrong. This occurs throughout the entire movie - events changed, things removed and added, all in order to whitewash Chris and his actions, and make America look like the good guy in an extremely complicated conflict. I think that in order for this review to have its desired impact, I need to add a bit of simple context surrounding the war, just to highlight how truly awful Chris was, and how the movie portrays him and the Iraq War. Estimates of the death count in Iraq vary wildly, but conservative estimates using only documented cases are over two-hundred-thousand. That figure becomes several times higher, over one million, when including indirect mortality caused by the likes of collapsing healthcare, infrastructure damage, malnutrition etc. Much of this damage was caused by aerial bombardment from aircraft such as F/A-18s, F-16s, A-10As, AC-130 gunships etc., which Chris discusses in his book calling them "awesome". He recounts a night in which Iraqis attempted to flee as they were torn to pieces by gatling guns: Fuck, I thought to myself, this is great. I fucking love this. It's nerve-wracking, and exciting and I fucking love it. He also explains the different groups operating out of Iraq: Some were former members of Saddam's army and members of the Ba'athist Party that Saddam had headed. There were Fedayeen, members of a paramilitary resistance group the dictator had organized before the war. There were small, poorly organized groups of Iraqi guerrillas, who were also called Fedayeen, though, technically, they weren't connected with Saddam's organization. Though nearly all were Muslim, nationalism rather than religion tended to be their primary motive and organizing principle. Then there were the groups organized primarily around religious beliefs. These identified themselves as mujahedeen, which basically means "people on jihad"--or murderers in the name of God. According to Chris, all these people deserved to die for fighting against the foreign invasion by the US, a country that imposed its will on the people of Iraq through extraordinary violence using the likes of the previously stated aerial bombardment, but also mass internment and torture. It is evidently clear from Chris's own words in both the book, and interviews discussing his time there, that he had zero qualms surrounding his actions in Iraq, yet the film makes him out to be some sort of tortured hero suffering from PTSD, haunted by his actions (which is an insult to those actually dealing with it). This again, is an attempt to make him more sympathetic. At no point in the book, or after, did Kyle ever express such feelings. As Frankie Boyle said: Not only will America go to your country and kill all your people, they’ll come back twenty years later and make a movie about how killing your people made their soldiers feel sad. Just take a look at how disgusting his words are when describing his killings: There's another question people ask a lot: Did it bother you killing so many people in Iraq? I tell them, "No". And I mean it. The first time you shoot someone, you get a little nervous. You think, can I really shoot this guy? Is it really okay? But after you kill your enemy, you see it's okay. You say, "Great". I loved what I did. I still do. If circumstances were different--if my family didn't need me--I'd be back in a heartbeat. I'm not lying or exaggerating to say it was fun. I had the time of my life being a SEAL. I never once fought for the Iraqis. I could give a flying fuck about them. And let's imagine for a moment that Kyle was indeed a hero. This movie would still be based on the words of a notorious liar. For instance, he claimed to have shot and killed two carjackers in Cleburne, Texas, at a gas station in 2009. He told a journalist that the police then showed up and ran his driver's licence. But instead of his name, address, and date of birth, what came up was a phone number at the Department of Defense. At the other end of the line was someone who explained that the police were in the presence of one of the most skilled fighters in US military history. The police then supposedly let him go without charge, and he said that he knew the tape was out there somewhere, because he would randomly get emails from police officers all over the country, thanking him for "cleaning up the streets". To me this reads as a "and then they all clapped" bullshit story, but thankfully journalists investigated these claims, and found that it was indeed bullshit. They checked with the medical examiner's office, which reported no such deaths in Cleburne in January 2009. They then asked Cleburne police about it and, after a day of research, they said they had no record of such a shooting. Same thing with the Johnson County district attorney's office. Incredibly, this isn't even his most egregious tale of his grandiosity. He told a story of the dire law-and-order situation following Hurricane Katrina, in which he and another sniper travelled to New Orleans, set up on top of the Superdome, and proceeded to shoot dozens of residents who were contributing to the chaos by looting. What kind of man proudly recounts a fictitious tale of him supposedly shooting thirty American citizens? This isn't to mention the lies he told about beating up Jesse Ventura, for which Kyle's estate lost the defamation case. The man was a serial fabulist, and the film followed in his footsteps by altering events in search of turning him into a hero. The worst part is that it all worked. It became the biggest war film, and his book was a New York Times number-one bestseller. This calls into question every aspect of the book and following film, particularly his kill count. He writes: The Navy credits me with more kills as a sniper than any other American service member, past or present. I guess that's true. They go back and forth on what the number is. One week, it's 160 (the "official" number as of this writing, for what that's worth), then it's way higher, then it's somewhere in between. If you want a number, ask the Navy--you may even get the truth if you catch them on the right day. This conveniently leaves room for the number to fluctuate, which it does, ranging from the 160 figure to 255, all the way up to 320 according to Kyle. None of his kills have ever been officially confirmed though, and given he's a bullshit artist extraordinaire, I'm pretty sceptical to say the least. However, he was caught lying about his decorations. In his book he claimed he received two silver stars and five bronze stars with valor. Yet his signed discharge form recorded two silver stars and six bronze. It was different again, once Navy documents were obtained showing only one silver star and three bronze. He was also reportedly warned before the book's publication that his medal count was wrong by a former commander who advised him to correct the claim before publishing, yet of course he chose not to do so. These embellishments should raise significant questions around his actions. One notable example that occurs in the film is when Chris kills a man supposedly carrying an AK-47, but the man's wife claims he was on his way to the mosque carrying a Koran. He was then investigated, but it was ultimately dropped. Yet there is a glaring omission in the movie. In his book he writes: The story was ridiculous, but the officer--whom, I'm guessing, hadn't been in Iraq very long--didn't believe me. The soldiers began to look around for the rifle, but by that time so many people had been in the area that it was long gone... I had trouble holding my tongue. At one point, I told the Army colonel, "I don't shoot people with Korans--I'd like to, but I don't." I guess I was a little hot. Well, after three days and God only knows how much other "investigation," he finally realized that it had been a good kill and dropped the matter. But when the regiment asked for more overwatches, we told them to fuck off. This is extremely worrying given that he claims a higher total of unofficial kills that nobody witnessed, seeing as his apparent rules of engagement were as follows: If you see anyone from about sixteen to sixty-five and they’re male, shoot 'em. Kill every male you see. How many innocent civilians did Kyle potentially slaughter beyond the purview of official investigations? And why does he like to change the number of kills so often? He says: The number is not important to me. I only wish I had killed more. Not for bragging rights, but because I believe the world is a better place without savages out there taking American lives. It supposedly isn't for bragging rights, but it certainly seems that way to me. He also admonishes Muslim Iraqis as being "murderers in the name of God" as he put it earlier and says: We don't kill people because they're a different religion. The people we were fighting in Iraq, after Saddam's army fled or was defeated, were fanatics. They hated us because we weren't Muslim. They wanted to kill us, even though we'd just booted out their dictator, because we practiced a different religion than they did. Isn't religion supposed to teach tolerance? This is ridiculous for two reasons. The first being that earlier, I included an excerpt in which he himself admitted that most Iraqis were fighting on grounds of nationalism rather than religious reasons. But now it's more suitable for them to all be "fanatics" to excuse his actions. And secondly, it's ironic as he says this: On the front of my arm, I had a crusader cross inked in. I wanted everyone to know I was a Christian. I had it put in in red, for blood. I hated the damn savages I'd been fighting. I always will. They've taken so much from me. This is already an extremely long review, and it may seem that I've put too much emphasis on Chris and his book, rather than the film at hand. But rather than go through each moment in the film, as I'm losing steam at this point, I'd like to harken back to the opening scene of the movie, where the woman hands her child an explosive. American Sniper deliberately retold this event to make said woman seem even more evil than how it occurred in actuality. If Eastwood were at all interested in making a critical film about war, rather than the propaganda it actually is, perhaps he might have included more nuance. Even Chris Kyle himself admits that: Insurgents normally put small rocks in the middle of the road to warn others where we were. Civilians usually saw the rocks and quickly realized what was going on. They always stayed far away. Hours might pass before we saw any people again--and, of course, by that point, the people we would be seeing would have guns and be trying to kill us". But instead of including anything of this sort, Eastwood, Cooper, and writer Jason Hall decided to put out a piece of propaganda denouncing the Iraqis and proclaiming Chris Kyle to be an American hero. In reality, he was just a cunt. As for Kyle's murder, I haven't a single ounce of sympathy for such a maniacal, disgusting, murderous piece of shit - a stain on humanity. Fuck Chris Kyle, fuck his book, and fuck this movie.

To be fair, American Sniper is a pretty well made film (apart from the fake baby), I found the action sequences entertaining, and Bradley Cooper’s performance was impressive given he’d mostly only been in comedies before it. The cinematography isn’t groundbreaking but there’s definitely attention to detail in the shot choices. My issues are with the screenplay. I found the strong theme of good vs evil with an unwaveringly heroic portrayal of America’s role in the Iraq war uncomfortable to watch. While bias isn’t inherently an issue, given the film is based on true events and the controversies surrounding such a significant war, I’d be concerned about someone watching the film who wasn’t aware of the context and details. His eagerness to kill (regardless of the validity of his motives) made it difficult for me to sympathise with Kyle. Furthermore, he comes across as even more unapologetically patriotic in his autobiography claiming that everyone he killed “deserved to die”. I personally find this troubling as a sentiment and wouldn’t choose to hail the person who said it to the extent Eastwood does in the film. I appreciate that since it’s based on a book, Eastwood is somewhat limited in shaping the narrative, however, I found the sequencing slightly messy and was disappointed by the dropping and ambiguity of various plot lines. I may not be the target audience for American Sniper and perhaps I’d rate it higher if I was from the US. But then I do think The Hurt Locker is an incredible film and that’s pretty American.

Once again Clint Eastwood doesn’t simply create a conservative-wet-dream here, even if sometimes in the discourse about this film, the idea might come up; I definitely disagree with the claim, that this is a glorification of the Iraq-war or any US-military operation in the western Asian area of the past 30 years. I think Eastwood simply tells the story of war from the perspective of a “brain-washed” American soldier and thus wants to us see, what someone sees, who was brought up with a rifle in their hands already and frightened by the media, who created the picture of the “dangerous Muslim terrorist” in the minds of Americans after 9/11. The central question to ask is: does Eastwood side with Bradley Cooper’s character or does he just observe his actions. When you think, that he sides with “Chris Kyle”, then this film is on the same territory as something like Michael Bay’s “Pearl Harbour”, where the US-Army is glorified. I don’t think that we are on such territory here. Through the direction and also through Cooper’s performance there is always a distinct rift between the viewer and “Kyle” as a character. Eastwood doesn’t allow us to fully identify with him. He is definitely depicted as a slightly weird guy, who is drawn into the entire topic of war and the horrors, that come with it and who also doesn’t really understand, what his actions really mean; he is someone, who cannot see clear about the horrors, that he commits, which is also why he doesn’t feel sorry. But that doesn’t mean that Eastwood himself wants us to be the same. For me this is — much like other Clint Eastwood movies, whose style of conservative filmmaking is (as I have pointed out recently in my review for “J. Edgar”) much more nuanced — an observers view on a system, where technically we should feel pity for those people, who are unable to see behind the curtain and fall right into the traps. Thus it’s also a bit dull to call this movie out for being too focussed on the American perspective and seemingly uninterested about the casualties that this man creates in Iraq. Eastwood simply doesn’t want to show this here; his focus is the story of a soldier’s life, that is destroyed by a war-machinery, that makes him believe to be heroic part of something, while eventually he’s just ammunition for the interest of someone else — kind of the idea that the first two acts of “Born of the Fourth of July” follows. This is also hauntingly shown, when “Kyle” is back home for a short time and shows his son to use a rifle, just like his father did. The cycle of violence won’t stop here, because these people are trapped in the world of serving someone else’s interests — something that’s incredibly far away from the ideology that I’d associate with Clint Eastwood. So all in all it’s a film about the lost lives of soldiers and as such it succeeds mostly. I decided to still give a rather mid rating, because for me the runtime is too long, especially since the story gets a little repetitive the longer “Kyle” stays in the war-zone. A higher focus on “Kyle’s” family life and the destruction of it would have made a better movie in my opinion, even if Eastwood is able to create some intense fighting scenes. But this should have been more like “The Best Years of our Lives” or “Apocalypse Now” and less like “Warfare”, because there’s no way that I won’t get bored at 130 minutes of people shooting around in the desert.

American Sniper works because it makes the story feel personal. The film is tense, well staged, and easy to become emotionally invested in. You are not just watching military operations from a distance. You are watching what those experiences do to the person living through them. That is what makes the film compelling. The action sequences are intense, but the quieter moments matter just as much because they show the psychological weight that comes with everything happening on screen. There is a constant feeling that the character is caught between two worlds. The battlefield. And home. And the transition between them never feels simple. That makes the story easy to connect with on an emotional level, even if the actual experiences are obviously far removed from everyday life. The direction does a good job of making the tension immediate. You understand the pressure of making decisions in seconds. You feel how quickly situations can change. And you understand why those experiences do not simply disappear when someone returns home. That emotional side is what stayed with me most. The film is not perfect, but it is gripping, well performed, and strong enough to make you care about the person at the center of it. A tense and emotionally engaging war drama that works best when it focuses on the psychological weight carried home from the battlefield.

​"Aim small, miss small." ​It is incredibly easy to see why this gets written off as the ultimate "dude-bro American propaganda" movie. It is intensely, unapologetically American, and it absolutely flattens a complex geopolitical conflict into a straightforward "America is the hero" narrative. You could go on for hours about this, and honestly, most of those critiques would be entirely well-placed. It’s also not a technically brilliant film—the pacing can feel incredibly choppy, the visual style is pretty flat, and yes, that notorious fake plastic baby completely pulls you out of the moment ​But if you dismiss it solely based on that surface-level wrapping, you're missing the forest for the trees. Despite those filmmaking flaws and the questionable depiction of America's role in the Iraq War, the movie still works because it succeeds entirely at what it actually set out to do: deliver a narrow, personal character study. ​At its core, this is about the psychological toll of deployment ​American Sniper isn't trying to be a sprawling macro-commentary on the ethics of the Iraq War. It’s about what happens to a human being when their entire reality shrinks down to the crosshairs of a sniper's scope. Clint Eastwood does a good job showing how the cumulative effect of these tours slowly erodes a person's ability to exist in normal civilian life with the time constraints that come with creating a Hollywood blockbuster ​The combat sequences are tense, aided by some incredibly sharp audio design, but the real hitter is the silence once Chris Kyle gets back to Texas. Bradley Cooper sells that weight, showing us a man who is physically sitting on his couch with his family, but mentally still scanning rooftops thousands of miles away. ​It’s wrapped in patriotic bravado and hindered by some clunky filmmaking, but underneath it all is a genuinely interesting look at the personal cost of trauma and duty. ​If you judge it by its true intent, rather than its politics or its technical polish, it does hits the target. ​All that said, it would be incredibly biased to completely dismiss the aforementioned flaws. They absolutely impact the viewing experience, and the film does require you to actively overlook some of its shortcomings in order to see the forest through what are, admittedly, some rather large trees. But if you can manage that, its true intent still shines. 3.5/5
